CAPTAIN MOONS, If Leo oe ('AWNPONE.—First among the hero. of Cawnpore must he named Cop to M. ore, of the 32nd, a man of light hair, blue eyes, and withal of coon- mandieg presence. Wherever there was must pressing tisk, : and wherever there was direst wretchedness, hi, pleasant presence was seldom long wanting. t7teler the rampart, at ' the batteries, in some ont-pieket where the non were drop- ping like IMeasents under a fearful cross-fire, in tome corner of thehoapital—to a brave heart more fearful still—where by the mangled forms of those young and delicate beings whom war should always spare, ever and everywhere was heard his sprightly voi.v speaking words of encouragement or eshor. tation, of sympathy, and even of courteous gallantry. Wherever Mmne had passel he left men something more courageous curl women something less unhappy. Brave and vivacious hincelf, he a-as the cause that bravery and • vaeity were in other men no evil mould wmry him. no danger daunt. It was not that he had lem at stake than lit-re around him, for Itin wife and children were in the en- , trenchments. Moore replied that he could spare nelmly hut Ithnself and Lieutenant Delafnese. At the deed .4 night he stole out front the entrenchment, with fifty picked non at his heels, in the direction of the chapel :end the raeket-court. Beginning from this point, the party hurried down the rebel lines under favour of the darkness, doing whatever rapid mischief was practicable. They amprised in untimely slumber some native gunners, who never waked again, spiked and rolled over neveral 241 pounders, gratified their feelings be blowing np a piece which had given them special annoyance, awl got back, carrying in their anne four of their number,,inot ITAV ing another behind. Iv the Peen§ are permitted to take matters easy, the Government has evidently made up its mind that the members of the House of COM MOOB, at all events, Mall have something to occupy their time with. Thin week a batch of important bills have berm introduced, and others of equal or grater importance tire promised to follow. 'We are indebted to Mr. J. G. tier Member for Warriogton, for Lamlen of the Bills introduced, and though we publish digitate of these in another column we shall be plemed to allow any one who desires to peruse the bill, them- selves to do to at the Warrieatou office of the E 1.011,111... The Registration of Voters Bill fur Ire- land is among the most important ef the Bills. By it it ia proposed to assimilate the borough franchise in Ireland to that which is oportviv. in England and Scotland, a measure that the late 00V8111011 net evinced no disposition to enewirage ttr to pass, though it wilt remove a great grievance with the Irish people. The prevent id males franchise in Ireland exeludee from the regixter of voters • vast number of oeitupiers of tenements, and this is borne out by the feet that though the Irish borough. return to Parliament thirty-one representatives the eleetora in the whole t of the boroughs number less thou the voters in one of our Lancaehire conatituenciea rot urniog three mote. hers. If the franchise in helmet is as-imitated to that of England it is °outmoded that in B Gam nlone the electoral body will be iucreased ft,te fifteen thousand to twenty-fire thousaud. The line at which the franchise is at present drawn 'nay seem very low ,! but in making comparison, it must be remembered that house property ix much cheaper in li.land than ! in England. Low att it may won the rata! qualifica- tion Imo the effect of denying to thous olds of house- holder. the franchise, while the occupant of every house in England, to matter what the ratal of his , habitation in, is qualified to La placed on the register.. Another important meseure the late Government endeavoured to settle, but did not—e ompensat ion for aocidents to workmen—the prudent Government hue taken in hand, and it is proposed to make employers responsible for inj units to workmen occasioned by the negligence of employero or servants I charged with the exerchie of any authority on their premiere. This bill haw been introduced by Mr. Dodson, and though it promittee to settle e mu:h- omed question it well no doubt elicit much criticism on the second reading. The forming industry are not to be left long in doubt of the mews of the msmures of relief the Premier, when in Opposition, led them to expect when the Liberals Moult again return to power. On Thursday eveuing the Home Secretary introduced into the Common, a bill " for the better , protection of the occupier. of I.d waited injury to: their crop. from hares and rabbits," and we doubt . not that tenant farmers whoos crop, are injured by these quadruped. will welcome as a boon this Bill, which will secure to them, instead of to tko lend. owner., the right to kill or to preserve the game. Bet the help to the toiling husbandmen is not to terminate with this concession. A bill is to be introduced by. the President of the Board of Trade to change the: method of taking the tithe averages, which has hitherto been far from mtisfactory to farmer.. The whole system of tithes will some day crop up for aboliticn, but that day is not yet at hand and what it now proposed by the Government is to do an act of juatiee to farmers. At present the averages are taken from the top of the market and are not really averages at all, as they simply repreeent the 'view the beat wheat fetches in the market. What is pro. posed is that no the tithe is levial on the whole the average price of the best grain should not be taken, but the price of the good, bad, and indifferent to- gether. A Sunday closing Am for Wales, the legal- ising of marriages with decearted 'vv.' sisters, the extension of the hours of polling, improved legis- lation affecting those engagel in seafaring hi. an amended mode of assessing house duty and the in- come tax, are all meaoures on which much public interest is centred. An effort is to be made to settle the Burials question. The prop.als of the Govern- ment are deemed to be 80 fair .1 equitable by one of the most popular dignitaries of the State Church, the Bishop of Mancheater, as to win his approval, and no doubt all but bigots will concur with that prelate in his opinion that it ought to be aneepted by all Churchmen. Them and other Government measures promised by the Government in the Queen's Speech, together with bills to be introduced by private members, will find t both the Commons and the Lords, who are to deal first with the Burial Lair!, plenty of work before the end of the session.

Mr. IL. B. Shores been appointed secretary to the Widnes Liberal Association, in the place of Mr. W. Bei ring- ton Jones, resigntd. The friends of the Rey. W. Robinson, f late Congregation-I alist,) mil curate of Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, will be glad tol,to.rtl,.at he has paserd his dual examination during the last week at Chester. "Ibe emirllllll.l4 were the Bishop of Cherer, the Archdeacon, Chancellor Espin, and Canon Grey, and when I have said this 1 think I have said enough to prove that Mr. Robinson's oath into the Entablah- ment, at least as for as his examination Was concerned, would not be one etrewn with roses. Let me wish him one thing, and that Is, that during the rest of the term of Ilia natural life he may never see the face of a college tutor mom —that it is in the shape of an inquisitorial examiner. Your Runcorn readsrs will be pleased to see that the Royal Humane Society have not been slow to recognise the brave act of Mr. Thomas W. Speabmin, of (hove House, that town, in rexuing a boy named Al trod Pye from drown- ing in the river, near the Ferry Slip, on the 3lst March. Some of the Wesleyan Methodism who are connected with the public life of Runcorn do not appear to Inc actuated with any t. much of the desire to follow out the advice of , the Apostle, and if they had any complaint of a brother to first go and tell it to Into, after which, Übe would not lister, patiently, it was to be told to the Church. For instance, Mr. Thomas Norio., poor law guardian, anti Mr. Wright,' relieving officer, sing the same hymns on a stintlay, hut tn a week day—at the usual meeting of the Board—Mr. Norman publicly charges an ohl officer like Mr. Wright with insulting An eidetly lady to whoo he has to give relief. Mr. Norman tam) say that lie has a duty to dis- charge to the public, but would it not Ink better in the e.. of those without" if such little matters as these were pilled by means of muteal explanations, or submitting them to one of tbe ministers of the denomination, rmher than one brother" doing that which is not very likely to exalt another in the eyes of the g. neral public Both the gentletnen moricerned have now nhlain,4l those grey hairs which are said to be a mown of aim., if found in the way 4of righteousness, anti a ith these mortis of maturity of wisdom there ought to he the finite " —peace, bov, totig suffering, ant a h.ost of othet virtues. in- cluding mutual forbearance. No doubt, in one sew, Mr. Norman in lidtn justified in the eour,e Ite has thoullit fit to adopt, hut is it a considerate one to an old officer ? I might also ask whether one would or oral lysuppose that an officer like Mr. Wright would willingly insult nay old lady?

It is rerstifyin4 to see that the Widnes Local Board appear to be determined to arson'', with the sewarag,e diffi- culty at w early date. The matter is now in the 'mods of Major Cross, the chairman of the Hotel, and I understand that the scheme is likelv tn he m,rtiod out aa enon.,t the requisite sanction is obtained from the Local Government Board.

The recent lamentable accident to a volunteer officer at Manchester ought to prompt all connected wit, the nervice to be doubly vigilant in the future. It ;a& wry easy matter for those in authority to order the titles to be overhauled and examined 1.4m1, and after every occasion when they are used, and this very simple means in all tlmt is i equited to prevent any mishap occurring. Officers have to face a danger when they c introut a body l men artned with titles, even though it be only at drill, and the late fatal occurrence shows how aciiiilente may hamn when lea,t expected. Thie is sufficient of itself to cause all volunteers to take every precaution in the I store. A number of enthusiastic Liberals have been worshipping at the shrine of II twanlen Castle. From what I hear, the entertainment as for as the things acceptable to the inner man are concerned, was not of quite no satisfactory a character as it might have been. FL kCCUS.

WOMAN BURNED TO DRAM AT DTMOR —A SAD CANI.-011 Saturday, an in inquest was held by Mr. C. E. Dritlield, county coroner, at the Blackburn Arms, Ditton, on the body of a 'MIMI n ante] Thomasine Wi nstanler, wile of John Winstauley, clogger, of Ditton Mill. The evidence showed on the evening of the Ilith inst., the deceanel an 4! her husband had had some drink. lie went to 13.1 early in the evening. awl left his wife sitting before the fire,l smoking. Alemt ten o'clock at night, he heard a scream, Ma some one knocking at the door. He went downstairs and found his wife in flames He tried to put out the fire by using his coat, and then opened the door, on which come of the neighbours ran in. div.head: WHITSUNTIDE _TRIP OtZi TIIE
div.p: WHITSUNTIDE _TRIP OtZi TIIE
Viitsff

lii, Often said that Englr:l:l;—n it:abroad In hot ro- Mantle scen,ry, while in their own country the,- ~r charm- ing picturesque landscapes equal to any thskro, h-I.,eseenon the Continent. It may also be mid that manWresidentson the hanks of the river Mersey travel miles in the eutumer time to mine watering place to breathe invigorating li,. when it can lie foetid within a few milet of their own doors at a very frilling expenee, tool that, too, on the tanks of thr Mersey. , To many people the Mermy is a stream whose watera are black m ink, whose banks are composed of solid mud, soil Whom, scenery consists simply of unsightly chemical works, frown which to many coloured enema into the river be- low. To not it has a very different aspect, flowiLg es it dam Jaye here and there, through a tract of country which i• exceedingly fertile, well womied, and interesting. Con- sequently it will not be surprioiog that I chose the river as the scene of my Whitsuntide holiday. With a plentiful supply of provisions I set off for l.aethem Ferry, which Is , situated on the Chenhire side of the river, about an how's toil inward front the Liverpool landing stage. Them,' joined two friends who had 0000110 doter front Warrington to a yacht, End who were bent on enjoyment. I immediately went on board. and having stowed away Inv belongings, I took, lord, around. Fatah., Ferry is delighdolly Mutated no the edge of a large wood. The shore rises perpendicularly a4.0nt20 feet, and just above us we observed tovering higher than the trees by which it was surrounded, the newly white- Sashed chimney of a refreshment house that was hidd,o from view. A Lttle further to the weer. opposite Iho landing- stage, stands • fine hotel, which command. an extensive view of the river, and a few yards still furthei went' Situated the Ferry A'allita, the, three places being the habitatiuns OD the spot. Stav—l am forgetting. The land- ing AA, itoclf is inhabited by a !geom., but whether it has been oertifirol as soitaide for a dwelling place by the medical einem of the district, I ant unable to say; and then there re the soologieal gardens in which dwell animals and fowl front all parts of the globe, I suppose, and of whose existence •0 3/0 reminded by the shrill cries of foreign birds and the unearthly noises produced by a bear. Withal Eastham Ferry looks "A gentle, lovely place," and one which only Recife to oecome better known to be more frequentol. Our captain suggests that it is time to make a move. Ins few minutes the mils are set, the anchor /retail 11, and with a Siff easterly wind we are on our way twastards, the sun Shining brilliantly in an almost cloudlemi sky. On we shoot past two curious shaped VPAPPiS with delicate looking masts from which fly red fig., and close by are several smaller weasels that also have red fla.is flying no their tn,t beads. nese are powder nimasintio in which it kept all the powder that is brought into Liverpool by vessels. Now we get amongst the shipping lying at aneFor, and after passing 000 or two landing stages we observe whst seem to be four dom- ing factories, but which in reality are four of the old o womlen call," of England, vessela which, after probably sailing in every wreen, strike coo,. having settled down 10 quietly end their days as training ships in the Mersey. What a contrast to the war ships of ti -day! Then, 110 m b. of thi shipbuilders war eviden m m tly ta make something to eliot at, now—nothing. We passed thme in a very short time, and came too number or meant shipa lying at anchor. On two of them RP readily distinguished the Manx Arius, aml were reminded of our visit to

Beautiful Mona, robed in ambient air.- In a few olin ea After we rapidly stiled past the Liverpool landing Wage from which steamers were flitting to and fro, giving the place an exceedingly lively appearance. To our sight for toile. are the Liverpool docks from which rise the lofty rigging of shipping from all quarters of the u odd. On le, left rides at anchor a hue iron vessel named the "Lassel," probably an American liner, and in another minute we leave behind the "City of Paris," of the lonian Line. Then ire pass what from her name we believe totes Dutch ship. A rope twirler is thrown over the ship's side, and we sae the Custom's boat swing round and come alonvide. A. we ran pretty clone to the vessel, one of the custom officers asked whence we hailed. Opposite New Brighton we caught sight et another Warrington boat, which hoisted sail. It followed ea for about an hour, and then put back. The u ind blew very strongly, and as the waves inereawd in size we began to pitch splendidly. We were now off the Crosby shore, where the trial t ips of new steamer, take place, and, having nothing else to do, we timed our run of the measored mile, which we did in fifteen minutes. This was very slow sail- ing, but it was owing to the wind, u hich was blowing astern, and not bring the one to show the nailing qualities of our boat. Some distance ahead we observed a °Mi.% object half submerged in the water just on the edge of the kink. We found it to be the wreek ot an iron vessel. We now sighted the Crosby Lightship, which we steered for, and in the distance we mw several large sailing ships beating tip the channel with the tide. We were soonaloncsidethe light- ship, which ins substantially-built vowel about the else of a barge, and is painted red. Sailing to windward, we threw a nen-simper to the keepers, who are caged up in the vessel for several days together, and must have a weary time of it, the monotony of the surging billows being ouiy varied by Oh. cry of the seagull or the churning q/ the water by Dome steamship. in reply to our captain, one of the keepers informed us that the wreck we had just poured was that of one of Messrs. Leyland and Co.'s steamers. So for all hail I been pleasant sailing with the breeze, but we now pat about, being out of sight of land, .11111 began to copes rience the full force of the wind. The white -crested waves rushed upon on in full tilt, nweeping our decks and covering tie as well ; but having donned our oil skim. we conk! with- stand the freaks of the billows to a certain extent. For several miles the spray at dines flew over our heads, 0. tshing in our faces' and making us feel rather uncomfortable. Presently a fine screw steamer overtook us, but we were unable to decipher her name or to make out whit line of steamers she telongal to. Then we arrival at the New Brighton rock where, as Longfellow bee it,— The lighthouse lilts Its mawlee masono A pillar of Ore by olalo, of cloud by day... The scenery at this poplar watering piccolo very pret,v. Sell consists mainly of gentlemen's !residences plsasantiv taunted amid the trees. We rapidly sailed by the oew Egre- mont pier, the Seacombe landing stage, the extensive Birkenhead docks, and the Woodside ferry, and made for I Her Majesty'. gunboat which bad recently arrived in the I river. Having hastily aurveyed it we made amiss the river, and nailing round o rock arrived in a most charming, calm, and secluded nook designated "Knott's Hole." ST. HELENS 13ICYCLE CLUB.

The fame of the St. Helens Bicycle Club is not confined to the town, the name of which the club bee, but is wide. spread, and Is known in different parts ..1 the country. It is admitted to be one of the best clubs in the kingdom, ranking. • •we believe, second or third in point of numbers. The , efficiency of tbeclubierenaarkable ; it containasome splendld riders, and nanubers lillongst its members some very reepeettd j and influential inrabitante of the town. The doings of the I club, the success it has attained, the many pleasant rides it I has had, will be familiar with most et our readers through ! the reports which we 11.1,10 from time to time published con.; corning the club, in these columns. Considering the standing of the club it is no wonder that the annual handicap races, and more especially the championship race, are looked forward to with a gr.t deal of interest not only , by the members of the club themselves, but by the great section of the St. Helenn public. For the p.t two years theno room have been run on the road bow -en St. Helens and Warrington, and on those occasions attracted a great number (of people to witness the proreedings. In many ways the holding of the races on the read proved disadvantageous the public were not able to one the whole of the races. and the various interesting even. such as two rival bicyclists alternately getting the lead, the fall of a stalwart from his Iron horse, the sweating and fuming of a wear-non b.other of the club, and other things that transpire in 000rneetiooneiehoonooitingtoo, The only persons f•rivileged to .e tine sports were those who owned their noble steeds," or sat at eaon in their wagonettes, traps, or shandries, end who followed the competitors on the ways. Another disadvantage to the club was that, in return for the pleasure they afforded. there was nothing in retuna. The club therefore acted lisely in deciding to hold the races on the cricket ground at Menton's Green. This was done of Wainesday night, when I about 2,000 persons paid for admission, amongst thou being I a goodly number of the gentler sex. The g.an.l-stand was l well patronised, and financially the annual races were al ]lroereofoftlme evening was, of course, the ehalapionship race, the winner being eolith,' to held the challenge cup, which has to be won three times before It becomes the property of 0 e winner. Mr. Middlehtesc is a well. keen.° bicyclist, bat &fore the close of the race it M. evi- dent he would not carry •ff the pahn again tide year. We ought to sty that the ground was in gmal condition (as goat as could be expected In a field', the , Irma.- was favourable, and it was neither too hot nor too cold. Soon after starting, which was shortly after eight o'clock, He position of the rider. was Meet, Middlehurst. Swift, and Whalley, the position being the same in the second lap. In the third lap kfiddleburst came first, followed by Meet, Swift, and Whalley, the position being the samo in the fourth lap. Swift then got first in the next half lap, hot waa soon passed by Middlehord. Swift, however, not I willing to be trifled with, made another spurt, and parsed the champion. This sort of thing was kept up between Widdlehirrat, Swift, and Mere for the tiret two miles. and it was doubtful which of those gentlernen would obtain the mastery. Whalley, who had been ateadily plying at the wheels. driving before hirn his three rivals, but who never lost any ! ground, at this point thought it was time to raise his energies, red, amidst the tremendous cheers of the ;mem,- tor% he glided in splendid style past black, blue, and red, leasing them Revere' yards behind. Many of the spectators had been predicting that the cup lay between Middlehurst, Swift, end Meta, but others choked their heads knowingly, and intimated that {Shelley would yet come from behind and make it warm for the others. Near the finish the crowd broke through Mto the ring, anxious to see the last of the race. 'HOCKING ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.' t On Monday an accident of • terrible character happened •,to an assisMnt engineer naintab Richard Owen Biddulph, ' aged 2.5 years, of Egertometreet. Runcorn, employed on the • ! steamer `'` Helen," belonging to the Bridgewater Navigation Company. Whilst the t 0,,, running between Liver- pool and Runcorn the &ceased removed the guards , protecting him from the beam of tbe engine, it is supposed for (ha object of getting Borne chips lying in the bottom of the boat, and whilst to engaged he was struck by the beam , and instantly killed. D,ceasedb, head was shockingly I mutilated. He leaves a svife and three chit Men. Judging from the evidence given at the inquest, which was held on ; • Tueolay afternoon before Mr. Worsloy, deputy coroner, at the Masonic Arms, Devonshire-square, fliddulph seems to . • have been an exceptionally nert and careful workman: and :! bin death must have resn!ted from forgetfulness of the banger in which he was placal "after haying removed the , guanle. Much sympathy is into for his widow and fancily. • Mt. bleadowcroft. the age, of the company at Runcorn, and Mr. Rawlinson, tw:perintentlent of the &eke, were , present during the inquest, at which the following evidence • , was given ! I Thomas Maddock, No. 2, Portland-street, Duke's Field, . Mreman on hoard the steamer "Helen," belonging to the Bridgewater Navigation Company, deposed that ou the 2401 • ! inst., about twenty to elever o'clock in the morning, he was !on oard the yeesel with tha captain, William tfailweosi, the ! deceased, Richard Bankes' Alfred (lough, and Chew Aepey. !it bw en last he so,, deceasel he wee in the stoke hole, nod old him (witness) to fetch a bucket, which he believed he required to dean out the lower engine house. He went into the upper engine house for the bucket, and w.occompanital , by deer eel. The engine driver was also in the upper engine house, but did not seem to observe thetn. He sa• . deeeased take up two plates near a side lever, and then i left him to go for some water. When he cancel . back, in about three minutes, he found that he • had got his head cut open. and he raised violators. He inc. • mediatetv told the engineer that something had happened ! to Bidthaph. The boat wa, in the Mere.y on its way to , Runcorn, between Hale-head and Weston l'oint, st the time the accident occurred —idol: rd Bankes, of it, Arthur-street, , I Park Moll-rood, Liverpool, sail he was engineer on the be d. i He deposed th.tt the last wim ess ran up to him on the morn. tog of the accident, and told him that the dec..tsed'a head 1, woo "in the engine." 11:, stopped the engine at once, and found ileceawd with his kat under the beam of the engine, and hin knees amidships. Decease•l's bead was frig, dully Icut, and he was quite dend.—ln answer to questions from the Coroner, as to how he thought the accident had s occurred, the witness stated that deceased was very cleanly t in his work, and one who never needed to be to'd to do any- . thing which required to be done. He was of oi ll ion that . deceased bad seen some chips lying in the bottom of the . boat, on! wished to remove them. Whilst arteinpting 10 .14. . this, he had been unmindful of the beam of the ermine which , s had struck him upon the head, and en caused hie death. It r was certainly part of his duty to remove the chips, but it . was the rule lode Ruch work when the vewsel had stopped. There could be nothing more done to freer off the beam of the engine, which was well guarded already. Thedeceased o had taken away the guard, before trying to remove the • chips. He bad seen deceased about tea minutes before the : accident happene,d.—ln 'maiming up, the Coroner referred to the facts stated in evidence., to the Cotnpany not de- ) siring their servants to do work of • similar nature to that icr which deceased won occapied at the time of the accident. ~ Ile said deceased appeared Co ?lave b.en a particularly more. ful, tidr. clean, sober, and respectable man—one who took o some pride in the manner in whic. hedid his work. It seemed . that Biddolplc 'mann, who, if he sow anything going wrong, would go a little out of his way to put it right.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting ol thie Bawd leas held on Thurs- 4ny afternoon. M. Bradshaw presided, and there were also preeent the Revs. Father Finegan, Father Clarice, Mow.. Brock, Brunner, Hartland, Shaw, Taylor, awl Denby (Clerk.)

The report of this committee, which was adopted on the motion of Mr. Brunner, seconded lty the Chairman, stated that during April there had been 107 people summoned be- fore them, of whom 73 were applicatMns for payment of free and 94 for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recommenled to be paid in 30 cases. There had been six prosecutions before the magistrates and a like number of convictions. PROPOSAL TO BSC. BATH YlCarrs 10 .HOLAR, The School Management Committee recommended that bath tickets be given as rewards of merit (at a cost not ex- ceeding £lO this year) to those children in stand sul 111. to NU., in boys and girls' schools, who have made 400 attend- ances during the yur, ending February, 1880. The num- ber of attendances to qualify for bath tickete to he increased by ten each year, until 430 .are required.” Mr. TATLOR proposed the adoption of the recommend. lion, and and for had had a consultation with Mr. Carey as to what charge would be made, and he found that it would be one penny per head for three Lours in the plunge-bath on a Saturday morning, coil one halfpenny for each towel. The speaker dwelt upon the importance of the art of swimming in the education of the young, and said he believed the ado, tion of the recommendation would prove of great value in improving the attendance at the schools, Mr. Bocce had pleasure in uconding the proposal, which seemed to him a etep in the right direction, ae it would act beneficially both as to the attendance and the promotion of cleanliness. Rev. Father Fixenae opposed the proposition. He took the objection that ASTOTMIHIH cc old not be considered part of eletnentary education, and said they might as well begin to teach cricket and horsemanship ae to teach it. He con- tended that it was not within the power of the Board to grant £lO for any such purpose. and be believed that no auditor would ever pass the account. The CHAIRMAN suggested that the better plan would be to leave the proposal over for a short time, ia order that enquiries might be inetituted as to whetter the Education Department would give their unction to it. Mr. TAYLOR eboogice they could just as reasonably give a reward of merit in the slmpe of tickets for the Lathe as they could give books. The Liverpool School Board had arranged for the sending of children collie baths in that coy. The Rev. Father FINEGAN, in the course of another short speech, said he thought no gentleman on the Board Scalia connive at breaking the law by any sinister method of admitting He children to the baths. They might just aa usily give a child a book and tell it to go to the office of one of the railway companies and it would receivl+ a ticket for New Brie ton or Buxton. The Board was now spending quite enough without entering into any doubtful kind of expenditure. He would advise his hiend Mr. Taylor to have nothing to do with any such t' Water Bill." (Laughter.) Mr. Tavxon : We have gel the water, sir. Mr. Snow thought it was a very important subject and one upon which they ought to take safe ground. They have hitherto been spending Loge sums in payment of the salaries of visitors, and the new proposal would be an experiment which might emoena benefit to the town. Ile certainly thought the plan would he an advantage, if it would not be contrary ton the provisions of the Education Department. They might write to the Department upon the subject. Mr. TAYLOR Do I understand that if the Education Department agreed to the proposal we might pass it when it comes before the committee ? If we are to fight now, let or have it out and vote upon it now. I don't want to be fighting each Baud day. Mr. 13111,1NYR If I voted now I should certainly he ia- cbnrd to vote against it. Mr. TAP.. : I might not think it worth tny while to make any farther enquiries. Mr. BRUNNBR: Then as far eelam concerned tbe matter might drop. It was resolved that the eubject should be referred back to the committee.

M. Bacot read the report of this committe:, which stated that they had received the half-yeailv statement of the architect's of the Board, on the various schools, and having examined the several buildings, they recommended that the repairs be effected, as per the architect's apecifications. lie proposed the adoption of the report. The Coratiocart seconded the motion which was passed.

site has been n'toiedmirably Chosen. files wooden erec- tion underneath the market shed, contiguous to stalls, Jr, and there is no doubt it will prove benefit and a con- venience to the numerous pedlars who attend our markets for whom it has been chiefly erected. At present it is only resolved to open the tavern on Market days, but in course of nine, if the scheme operates successfully, will be opened daily. There wale good Influx of customers on tbe day of opening, and at half.paat three the Mayor (J. R. Pickenere, Esq.) attended to formally open the same. There were also the following present i'—Mrs. Charles Broadbent, Alderman Device, Councillors Pairelough sod Wallingten, Mr. Clmr- ley, Rev. Mr. Schonberg, Mr. T. Morris (chairman of the company), Mr. Bow • don, r. 11. Roberts, Mr. Siddall, Mn. Tote, Mr. Jones, and Mr. W. Roberts. The Mayon said he had been asked to come there that afternoon, and he did tio with great pleasure because he be- lieved that of all institutions founded in that cuuntry for the good of the working classes, the cocoa and coffee houses were undoubtedly pre-eminent. Tiwy were made for the million, and he believed the million really enjoyed them. Before the existence of such iustitutions people who did not want to enter public-houses and get been were obliged to quench their thirst at public water founwine, and he was sure the institution of such houses of refreshment would be duly appreciated by the working population to whom they would lie a great benefit, lie hoped that Mr. Morris and his friends who bad been the promoters of those Institutions in Warrington would find that they became increasingly popular, and that they would he a p tying concern. No doubt they did not wish to make a large profit, but it the houses paid their way it would hot satisfaction to ail concerned. When a youth he re- membered most istintable lady who said she liked now because he was fond of tea. (Langhter.) Ile liked to see young men fond ot their tea—(bear, hear)—and he only wished that the labouring population of that town when they felt exhausted would avail themselves of the benefits ,t 1 that place, inasmuch as they could come to a clean and comfortable place and enjoy themselves to their heart's win- tent at a light expense. (Neer, hear.) It was a pleasure to see the cleanliness that characterised those institutions, an that went a great deal towards their success, for nobody liked Co take a nautirr a dirty place ; and if he passed that place and saw everything se nice and clean as at present, would not hesitate to call and take a cup of tea. (Cheers.) He did hope that the people of the town would find out that such places Were cut out for them, where they could have everything clean awl cheap, and that such institutions would Bullish, and the dheetors would have a prosper°us year lie had pleasure in declaring the lionto duly opened. (Loud cheers.) Mr. Mounts, as chairman of the British Workman Public- house Company, Mill he had much pleasure in asking the company to pass a vote of thanks to the Mayor for his kindness in opening that institution. •ft had long been his aim, .d that of Mr. Broadbent's .pecielly, to have apiece like that in the market, so that the market people could have the refreshments they needed ate light cost. They all knew the uncomfortable situation that 11131,1Speople were sometimes placed in to get refreshment, d the opening of that place would be a bene It to them. He regretted to say that several thnes the institutions of their company in Warrington hod been condemned by a class of people as gambling houses, and insinuations had been held forth that gambling wasaleo encouraged on their premises. lie should like it said that they had no more preventative of that, than what they had in the public-housos. They could not do anything that other people were forbidden to do in public business, and so Ice as gambling was concerned it was checked on their premises as much an possible. (floor, hear.) He was glad leery th.d those places were tombst more for the accom- modation of the workinz classes than for a profitable speculation, end he believed they net the requirements of those classes of the population. thing was to be done. Barret. Asserce.—Patrick Oray' , an hiAlunan, living in Bull's Read Yard, Bridge-Brent, was charged with being drunk and disorderly the print. Saturday afternoon, and ansaulting Catherine Farrell.—Sergeant Spinks said that on the previous Setunlay afternoon In was going home, when his attention waa called to a row that /tangoing on in Bull's Head Yard. When he got there he found the prisoner drunk and assaulting the prowcutrix. Farrel was insensible (rent the injuries she had received, and it took witness about an hour to bring her to a conscious condition. She was bleeding heavily from the mouth.—Prosecutrix stated that the prisoner kicked her in the mouth, and hit her on the head with a brick.—Prisoner denied the assault.—The Mayor said that front the evidence it appeared he had been guilty of moA cowardly conduct towards the woman. and aa the magistrates were determined to non such conduct. the prisnner would be sent to Walton Gaol for three months with bard labour.

Gibenn's work, Cli urch-street, were chargfd "for that on the 21st May instant, enter the premi.a of Moser.. Gihson and Son. and unlawfully did hide five chisel., two gauge, one rabbit plane, to deprive or hinder one Edward Cawley in the use thereof, and did wilfully damage a certain mallett at the sanse time." Mr. Harrieton defended the prisoners.—Edwd Cawley, o workman at Messrs. Gibson'., identified the tools his property, except the rabbit plane. n Thursday ' night last he loft the shop about half-past five. On Friday morning he went to the chop and found that his foot, in winch he had put the tools, had been broken open. On looking in the box he found that several of his toole wete missing. The mallet wan in good condition on Thursday night, but on Friday morning it woe broken in two.—Chief , Constable Hunt stated that when the prisoner George was lob:peed, he offered to show where the tools were hidden. In company with a policeman be went I) the works, end the labourer produced the table—Mn. Harrison pleaded guilty on WWI of George and Rigby, but said there was no case agaiest lA.—Chief Constable Hunt also said there was Hale or nothiog egainst Lea—The Bench .lischarged the prisoner I,a. Addressing the other prisoners, the Mayor said that they considered what they had done to be a serious matter, Ingot the name time bdieved that they had done it thoughtlessly. Thy did not wish to send them to prison, but they would have to pay a tine of 10s, and costs each. A DISHONEST BED-FELLOW_—Salnuel Wright, stated in the charge sheet to I, residing at Liverpord.road, Warring- ton, was brought up in custody on a charge of stealing from the trowsers pocket of Charles Burrows, the sum of Ils. and a breast pin and a pocket knife; from the pocket of Basil Muir,* the eum 8,1 ,• and AlB,l from the pocket of Jos.-ph Wateon the corn,,! 8s dd. It appeared that the prosecutors and prisoner elept at the house of George Gould, Bank Quay. on Saturday night last, endow getting up in the morning the osecutors lost dift.reIIISLIIIIS of money out of their pockets. The ordiee were communicated with, and under the mattress of the bed where the prisoner bad been sleeping, two donna were hidden. The prisoner, on being taken to the etation, dropped a gold pin in the road, which Burns identified as hie. The Chief Constable stated that one of the pro.cutors had written to him stating that he could not appear that day to prosecute, but would do so on the following Saturday if the case was remanded. DISPUTE AS TO A SUPPLY OF WATES.—The Warrillgloll Waterworks Company wei e summoned by Menu.. Robinson, Son, and Skinner, flint glass manufacturers, Warrington, for refusing to I urniell at the request of complainants a supply of to the dwelling-house of one Thoinas O'Nield, of Factory.lane. The caw. which merely involved a legal [...ideality, occupied several hours. Mr. Haywood, bar- rister, of Nlancheeter (instructed by Messrs. Jeans and Co., solicitors, Warrington), appeared Ce behalf of the complain- ants ; and Mr Taylor, teurister, Manchester (instructed by Mess.. Mich.., White, an I Nicholson, so:icitors, War- rington), defended the company.—Mr. Ilaywo.l, in opening the enne, said that the complaint was made under section 63 of the Warrington Waterworks Act, 1855. The only ques- tion to he decided was whether the occupier of a lodge attached to the works of the complainants was to be con- etrued an the occupier of a "private dwelling-house." Prior to December, 1877, Messrs. Robinson, Son, and Skinner, the owner. of the property in question, were in the habit of getting water (pan the Warrington Waterworks Coinpany for the urn of the man dwelling at the lodge, the men at the works, aid for trade purport.. Itt December, 1877, the con. plainants ceased having water from the company, they find-1 ing that the water from the River Mer.y suited them much 1 better for their trade, but retained the supply of water to I the lodge. Soon after that supply wig cut off also, and the reason why they refu.d to supply water to the lodge was that it was not a private dwelling house as defined by the Act. The only question raised was whether the lodge in ques6on was a dwelling house under the meaning of the Act, because, if eo, the Comdany would be forced to supply water thereto. William Robinson of the firm of Mews. Robinson and Skinner, said that up to December 1877, the debutante slipplied them with water. After that they ceased to take water from the Company, and their sup- ply was cut off. Id°. Taylor for the defence contended that the lodge in roost) on could not be construed into a "private dwellinghoune." inasmuch, as the occupier did not hold it by tenure. It was merely a place that O'Nield occupied in- older to open the gates of the works, and be on the spot al, ways. Ile apprehended he was not a tenant, because a tea' of tenancy was whether he paid rent or not. The Clerk It does not nay tenant in the Act of Run unent; it says ocche pier. I shall advise the magistrates that the information in laid under emotion 36 and that all other sections quoted do j not apply. Mr. 'Taylor continuing, said the the supply of water to the lodge was not out off from malice, but simply becauee there was an nodoe consumption, and called Mr. , Rona the secretary to the company, who proved that there had been on undue consumption at the lodge, and he had ordered it to be cut off because of it. The Clerk said he ahould advi. the Bench that there could not have been an undue consumption except with a knowledge on the part , of the connumer.—This concluding the ca., the Bench retired, .d, mm their ...appearance, the Mayor raid that it appeared to the Bench that O'Neild was the occupiers( the , house within the terms 01 1100 Act and entitled to the supply lof water asked for.—'The Clerk What about the penalty F- -1 Mr. Haywoul: We are willing to take a nominal penalty.— ; The law says the penalty shall be 210 and 40s. • day for , every day the offence has been committed.—Mr. Taylor was 1 of opinion that the penalty 0001,1 be mitigated one fourth, 1 but the Clerk said he did not know of any exieting statute , permitting such a couree.--The Mayor' The magistrates do 1 not wish to indict the penalty if they can help it—Mr. Taylor said Ile should appeal againat the decision of that court and the Butch then inflicted a fine of One, the coste to foPow the ...tin the usual coon.. J Ridgway appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr Preston rep, eented the defendants—Mr. Ridgway, in opening the case, stated that on the Bth March laet it waa Crewe fair. Al that fair the plaintiff bad certain cattle, and when the fair was over a cow, bull, and small pony retnained unsold. The plaintiff wished to have these animate brought home, and accordingly in company with his brother, James Rowbothain, took them from the fair ground to the London and North. Plaintiff paid the dues which were demanded from lib% and the animals were all loaded there by the servante of the Co opany at Crewe station. From what he had sent before the animals ought to have arrived at Lemrn the same evening. However, they did not arrive until the nest day at eleven o'clock. His brother James was there to receive thou, but on going to the truck he found that the bull was lying in some straw with its shoulder broken. The pony and CM although badly damaged, he received, and took them home. The plaintiff and hie brother would prove that when the I cattle were loaded at Crewe the bull was in a sound condi- I tinn so for as limbs were concerned, and for ought he (Mr. Ridgway) knew, it was sound in every other respect. When the bull no, loaded it was loaded like other animals. There wan no straw nor any packing of any description required, nor did they Imo any about him, but on the arrival of the , boll at Lyinni station It was found in thisinjurtid condition,' of no use at all, and they refused to receive him. From a letter which he (Mr. Ridglvayi bail received from the cattle manager el the London and North.. Preaton mid Mr. Ridgway had opened the contract as common carriers, when be must know there wan a special contract. —The plaintiff was then called, and he supported the maternent made by his solicitor.—ln °roes-examination by Mr. Preston, the plaintiff said the bull was a little footsore, but he never Saw it lying down in the truck.—James Rowbotham,' brother of the plaintiff, deposed to seeing the cattle loaded at Crewe, when they were in good condition. On 0 arrival of the cattle at Lymm, the bull was lying in the middle of the truck, with ite shoulder broken, and the cow was "knocked all to pieces."—His Hon ‘ur:Said that wee a metaphorical expression, hut be supposed it wee not all in I bits. Its shoulder was broken in several parts. He bought the bull for 15s.—This [ was the caeo for the plaintiff.—Mr. Preston said thie was a special contract, and if he could show that during the time ; of transit there war no rough Shunting, then he would be ' entitled to his Honour's verdict—His Honour said surely the contract did not relieve the company of ordinary ' liability as carrier', except as regarded the porn—Mr. Preston handed his lionoura contract signed by the plaintiff, by which, he contended, the cattle as well or the pony were ; to be carried at owner's risk.—llis Honour, however, held that the contract included only the pony,when Mr. Preeton called attention to the conditions.—His Honour, atter reading thein, said that by the special contract it was clear that the i animals must be carried at owner's riak, but, scondly, condi- ! lion I referred to cares only where the owner or servants r travelled with the animals conveyed, but in this Cl. neither , the owner nor him servants travelled with the animals, nor I contracted to do so.—Mr. Penton With that decision it lands me in the common law liability of carriers V—llis Honour : Yes—Mr. Preston But I suppose that as regards the bull we are insurers under any condition V—His Honour , I think en—Mr. Preston: If so, I must withdraw from the case. There is evidence about Inct animol's state when it was loaded, and I shall go that for and if before it was loaded it was in a bad condition I will leave it there, sir, and not puma it any further.—llis Honour: Very well.— Thomas Latham, cattle loader at Crewe Station, said when the bull was at Crewe it was lying down in the pen. When ! the cattle were loaded he made out a slip for the plaintiff to get the animate booked and he (witness wrote on the slip of caner that one of the animal, eras lame. He told the plaintiff the annuals must be tied up, when he replied, they wanted no lying up, as they would out stand and wanted to lie down.—John Buckland gave nimilar evidence. —His Honour thought the defendante were insurers, and es I there was no evidence to show that the bull was in a lead condition when loaded, he gave a verdict for the plaintiff for the amount claimed. J. Morphet, a young lady residing at Silverlands, Bowdon. near Manchester. Miss Morph. was !going on a visit to her friends at Soihurch, owl travelled !by train front Manchester. She asked a porter to take her trunk into tier left-luggage office whilst she went into the town, but he told her it would be all right on the platform, and the trunk was allowed to remain there. -ALLOOD Santo:q.t.:o.—A respectably drmsed young man, almot 20 years of age, who on the 6111 of April obtained , three gold watches and three guards, valued at £B5, frorn . Mr. Frederick Johnson, srateliniaker and elk...month. Bow- don, has been apprehended at It now, in Derbyshire. The prisoner, who gave the name of Jelin Herrington, lived iit , apartments in Bowdon, and introduced himself to Mr. John- : eon as a young man in redimed circumstances and offered to sell him his watch. Mr. Johnson declined to buy the watch, : hut the prisoner called several times on different days, and eventually the prisoner told Mn. Johnson that he had been !appointed an agent to Mn. Henry May, wholesale dealer in I jewellery and fancy goods, Birmingham, and that he sold . ,on commission. He hot several friends. and if Mr. Jobe- son would allow him commission he would mil a number of ' articles for him. He called neat day and mid that a friend of his wanted a watch and chain to cost some £25 or £3O. Mn. Johnson took the goods by the prisoner's request to bin !apartments, but he was mme half an hour late, and prisoner said hos friend had gone across home, and he wanted the prisoner to bring them across for approval. Mr. Johnson let him take the watches and chains, which were worth £ll5, • and as the prisoner did not come back he went to the police j office. The prisoner, who was brought before the Altrinchain 1 magistrates on Monday, was comnaitted for trial. After , leaving Bowdon the prisoner went to Manchester, where be j obtained a horse and trap and proceeded towards Maccles- field. He spent a week end at Mr. Lee's farm at Rainow, : and he told Mr. Lee that his name was William Sanderson, and that his father was a druggist in York-street, Chmtham. After staying from the Saturday to the Monday the primner , said that he would write home, but Mr. Lee noticed that he !did not post the letter, and then he thought there was some- I i thing wrong. Mr. Lee demanded the money for his keep , and that of the horse, whereupon prisoner gave him "loin" watchguard. The prisoner was neat beard of at Earl Seem- dale, in Derbyshire, where be put up the horse and trap at the Qiiiet Woman Inn. It was them a week, and prisoner lodged at a Mrs. Hall's. The landlady of the inn suspect- ing that the prisoner was about Cu go off without paying, her • daughter locked the stable door, and refused to let the horse Igo unl se payment was made. Eventually he gave them I one of the gold watches, saving that he was corning back at night to pay Mrs. Hall and he would call and pay then. The prisoner Ints arrested on Thursday on the charge of stealing the horse and trap in !danclimter. Tiro of the watches and two chains were found in his possession.
